title: Permutations of multisets
key_idea: For permutations of a multiset $M = \{1^{a_1},\ldots,m^{a_m}\}$, the inversions generating function is the $q$-multinomial coefficient $\binom{n}{a_1,\ldots,a_m}_q = \binom{n}{\mathbf{a}} = (\mathbf{n})!/((\mathbf{a_1})!\cdots(\mathbf{a_m})!)$. The $q$-binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k}_q$ also counts $k$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ and partitions fitting in a $k \times (n-k)$ rectangle.
summary: This section generalizes inversions to multisets: Proposition 1.7.1 gives the $q$-multinomial coefficient formula. The second proof uses standardization (a powerful technique for reducing multiset problems to set problems). Proposition 1.7.2 counts subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ via a direct analogy with the binomial coefficient. Proposition 1.7.3 (via row-reduced echelon form) connects $q$-binomials to partitions fitting in rectangles.

notation.description: q-multinomial coefficient: GF of inversions on $\mathfrak{S}_M$
# partitions of $n$ with at most $k$ parts, each $\leq j$

definitions.statement: Let $M = \{1^{a_1},\ldots,m^{a_m}\}$ be a multiset of cardinality $n = a_1+\cdots+a_m$. Define the **q-multinomial coefficient** by $$\binom{n}{a_1,\ldots,a_m}_q = \frac{(\mathbf{n})!}{(\mathbf{a_1})!\cdots(\mathbf{a_m})!}$$ where $(\mathbf{k})! = (1)(1+q)\cdots(1+q+\cdots+q^{k-1})$. The **q-binomial coefficient** is $\binom{n}{k}_q = \binom{n}{k,n-k}_q$, satisfying the Pascal recurrence $\binom{n}{k}_q = \binom{n-1}{k}_q + q^{n-k}\binom{n-1}{k-1}_q$.

A **partition** of $n$ is a weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda = (\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots \geq 0)$ of nonneg integers summing to $n$, written $\lambda \vdash n$ or $|\lambda|=n$. We say $\lambda$ has $k$ **parts** if $k = \ell(\lambda) = \#\{i: \lambda_i > 0\}$.

The **Ferrers diagram** of $\lambda$ is a left-justified array of $n$ dots with $\lambda_i$ dots in row $i$. The **Young diagram** uses squares instead of dots.

propositions.title: Inversions GF for multiset permutations
propositions.proof_sketch:
**First proof (induction):** Denote the LHS $P(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$. Remove all 1's from $w$: the remaining permutation $w'$ of $M' = \{2^{a_2},\ldots\}$ has $P(a_2,\ldots,a_m)$ inversions GF. The $a_1$ 1's contribute inversions depending on their positions, giving the $q$-binomial factor. The recurrence (1.69)-(1.70) follows, proving the formula.

**Second proof (standardization):** Map $(w_0, w_1, \ldots, w_m)$ with $w_i \in \mathfrak{S}_{a_i}$ to a permutation of $[n]$ by replacing $a_i$ $i$'s in $w_0$ by the elements specified by $w_i$. This gives a bijection preserving inversions up to a sum formula (1.71).

propositions.title: Subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ and $q$-binomials
propositions.statement: The number of $k$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ is $\binom{n}{k}_q$.
propositions.proof_sketch: Count ordered $k$-tuples of linearly independent vectors: $N = (q^n-1)(q^n-q)\cdots(q^n-q^{k-1})$. Each $k$-dimensional subspace $W$ has $(q^k-1)(q^k-q)\cdots(q^k-q^{k-1})$ ordered bases. Hence $G(n,k) = N / ((q^k-1)\cdots(q^k-q^{k-1})) = (\mathbf{n})!/((\mathbf{k})!(\mathbf{n-k})!) = \binom{n}{k}_q$.

propositions.title: q-binomial coefficient and partitions
propositions.statement: Fix $j, k \in \mathbb{N}$. Then $$\sum_{n \geq 0} p(j,k,n)\,q^n = \binom{j+k}{k}_q,$$ where $p(j,k,n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$ with at most $k$ parts, each part $\leq j$.
propositions.proof_sketch: Partitions fitting in a $k \times j$ rectangle biject with $k$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^{j+k}$ in row-reduced echelon form (Prop 1.7.2). The lattice path through the Young diagram traces the subspace, with $q^{|\lambda|}$ encoding the free entries of the echelon matrix.

examples.title: Standardization example
examples.content: Apply the standardization $\phi$ to $(w_0, w_1, w_2) = (21331223, 21, 231, 312)$.
examples.solution: Convert: 11 (in $w_0$) become elements $w_2(1), w_2(2)$; 22 become $w_2$-rearranged, etc. Stanley gives the example $(21331223, 21, 231) \mapsto 42861537$. And $\text{inv}(42861537) = \text{inv}(w_0) + \text{inv}(w_1) + \text{inv}(w_2) + \text{inv}(w_3)$ by the bijective formula (1.71).

examples.title: Partitions in a $2 \times 3$ rectangle
examples.content: List all partitions fitting in a $2 \times 3$ rectangle and verify $\binom{5}{2}_q = 1+q+2q^2+2q^3+2q^4+q^5+q^6$.

exercises.statement: Prove the $q$-Pascal recurrence $\binom{n}{k}_q = \binom{n-1}{k}_q + q^{n-k}\binom{n-1}{k-1}_q$ combinatorially using subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$.
hints: Condition on whether the last basis vector $e_n$ is in the subspace.

text_passages.text: Inversions in a permutation of a set extend to multisets: $(i,j)$ with $i < j$ and $w_i > w_j$ is an inversion of $w \in \mathfrak{S}_M$. Note we need the 4-tuple $(i,j,w_i,w_j)$ since equal elements can appear.

text_passages.label: Definition — q-multinomial coefficient
text_passages.preview: $\binom{n}{a_1,\ldots,a_m}_q = (\mathbf{n})!/((\mathbf{a_1})!\cdots(\mathbf{a_m})!)$ where $(\mathbf{k})! = [1]_q[2]_q\cdots[k]_q$. At $q=1$ this recovers the ordinary multinomial.

text_passages.label: Proposition 1.7.1 — Inversions GF
text_passages.preview: $\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_M} q^{\text{inv}(w)} = \binom{n}{a_1,\ldots,a_m}_q$. Two proofs: induction on multiset structure, and standardization bijection.

text_passages.text: The $q$-binomial $\binom{n}{k}_q$ is a polynomial in $q$ with nonneg integer coefficients. At $q=1$ it equals $\binom{n}{k}$. It counts both $k$-dim subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ and partitions in a $k\times(n-k)$ rectangle.

text_passages.label: Proposition 1.7.2 — Subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$
text_passages.preview: # $k$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ is $\binom{n}{k}_q$. Proof by double-counting ordered bases: analogous to the standard binomial coefficient proof.

text_passages.label: Proposition 1.7.3 — Partitions in a rectangle
text_passages.preview: $\sum_{n\geq 0} p(j,k,n)q^n = \binom{j+k}{k}_q$. Partitions in a $k\times j$ box are in bijection (via row-reduced echelon form) with subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^{j+k}$.

text_passages.label: Definition — Partition and Ferrers diagram
text_passages.preview: Partition $\lambda \vdash n$: weakly decreasing nonneg integers summing to $n$. Ferrers diagram: rows of dots (or Young diagram: squares). $\ell(\lambda)$ = number of parts.
